Abstract
The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles, by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

Conclusion
In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention.
For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers. On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles.
We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video.
Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours.
The code we used to train and evaluate our models is available at
https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor
.

papers.title: GPT-6-Astra Understands Touch and Outperform Vision--Tactile--Language--Action Models
papers.title_zh: GPT-6-Astra理解触觉并超越视觉—触觉—语言—动作模型
papers.abstract: General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability. Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8\% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31\% to 99\%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.

Introduction
The role of general-purpose large models in robotics is expanding
from task planning and skill selection
(
Brohan et al., 2023
)
and control program generation
(
Liang et al., 2023
)
to direct action decisions. Recent evaluations of GPT-6-Astra
show that a general-purpose multimodal model can generate
numerical robot actions from observations, task instructions,
and execution history, using feedback to determine subsequent
behavior
(
Team et al., 2026a
)
.
These studies progressively connect general knowledge to robot action,
raising a fundamental question: do general-purpose multimodal models
grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions, and can they
apply that understanding to guide their actions? Exploring this
question requires examining how models reason the physical
consequences of their actions and use interaction feedback to adjust
subsequent behavior
(
Huang et al., 2022
;
Liu et al., 2023
)
.
Tactile understanding provides a representative test case for a model’s grasp of physics, because interpreting tactile feedback involves making sense of physical phenomena such as contact, deformation, and constrained motion. We therefore choose contact-rich tasks such as insertion and alignment as our experimental setting
(
Huang et al., 2025
;
Bi et al., 2026
)
. Even after identifying a target and reaching the contact location, a robot can be obstructed by local pose errors and hidden geometric constraints
(

;
Xue et al., 2025
)

(
Chen et al., 2026
;
Higuera et al., 2026
)
. In this setting, tactile feedback allows us to examine whether models can connect the observed physical effects to their own actions and use that understanding to guide subsequent control.

Conclusion
To enable general-purpose multimodal models to use contact feedback for action adjustment, we present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy,
which combines expert-derived task guidance with online tactile observations. Expert experience provides task guidance for contact assessment and manipulation adjustment.
Online tactile feedback provides evidence for evaluating action outcomes and selecting subsequent adjustments.
Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves overall performance comparable to state-of-the-art policies across five UniVTAC tasks, matching or exceeding the compared methods on selected tasks.
Tactile ablation and execution analysis further demonstrate the role of contact feedback in local probing, directional adjustment, and restoring progress after obstruction. These results establish explicit task knowledge combined with online interaction feedback as an effective route to efficient contact-rich manipulation.

papers.title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
papers.title_zh: VecTile：一种面向三自由度力感知的低成本柔性触觉阵列
papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.

Jian Hou
Xin Zhou
Adam J. Spiers
†

Abstract
Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone.
Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force.
We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing.
VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns.
The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4
$\times$
4 array.
We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments.
In controlled single-taxel tests over 1–5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces.
A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use.
Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
I
Introduction
Tactile sensing gives robots a sense of touch during manipulation. It reveals force, friction, stiffness, and other properties that are difficult to infer from vision alone
[
1
,
2
]
. This information is particularly important for grasp-stability estimation
[
3
,
4
]
, object recognition
[
5
,
6
]
, and in-hand manipulation
[
7
,
8
,
9
]
.
During manipulation, the normal-force component captures only part of the contact state. While the shear components reveal the direction and magnitude of tangential loading, supporting grasp-stability assessment, friction and slip reasoning, and contact regulation
[
10
,
11
]
. Flexibility is also important because conformable tactile skins can cover non-planar and adaptive surfaces, including rounded fingers and soft grippers
[
12
,
13
]
. Because direct contact exposes tactile sensors to wear and damage, low cost and repairability are important for practical deployment
[
14
,
15
]
.
These considerations motivate tactile skins that combine 3-degree-of-freedom (DoF) force sensing, flexibility, and low cost. Existing tactile architectures, however, trade among these properties due to fabrication and integration complexities
[
2
]
: Vision-based
[
11
,
16
,
17
]
and magnetic-based
[
10
,
15
]
sensors can recover rich multi-axis contact information but are rigid, while thin capacitive
[
12
]
and piezoresistive
[
13
]
arrays more readily conform to curved surfaces yet do not provide shear force information. An easily accessible flexible tactile array providing local 3-DoF force measurements therefore remains underexplored.
We introduce VecTile (Fig.
1
), named as such due to its capability of reading a 3-DoF force vector at each tactile pixel (taxel). VecTile is a low-cost, flexible,
$6~\mathrm{mm}$
-thin,
$4\times 4$
tactile array (16 local 3-DoF taxels at a
$10~\mathrm{mm}$
pitch) that combines a piezoresistive array with passive silicone nubs.
Fig. 1:
VecTile on Fin-Ray type fingers during plug insertion. Color denotes normal response and arrows indicate shear magnitude and direction.
The complete sensor and readout board cost less than 35 USD (of which 25 USD is spent on an Arduino Nano that can be replaced with a lower-cost microcontroller and ADC circuit if needed). Raw frames stream at 343 Hz, and the measured end-to-end latency relative to a commercial force/torque (F/T) reference is approximately
$25~\mathrm{ms}$
. Most conveniently, this sensor can be easily produced in-house without the need for expensive equipment or tools. At its core is a combination of a standard flexible PCB (FPC), whose fabrication can be out-sourced at low cost (we used JLCPCB’s services) and silicone parts that can be easily produced via 3D printed molds (we used PLA molds fr

Conclusion
We introduced VecTile, a flexible
$4\times 4$
tactile array that recovers three-axis force at each taxel using passive silicone nubs to convert shear into a measurable pressure difference across four piezoresistive quadrants. The design requires no specialized fabrication equipment beyond a 3D printer and a hobby-grade vacuum chamber, and costs under 35 USD per unit (under 15 USD with a cheaper microcontroller). Finite element analysis showed that normal and shear loading remain mechanically separable and that nub height primarily controls shear gain; hardware experiments confirmed this, with the 3.0 mm design reaching 0.39 N normal and 0.16 N shear RMSE over 1–5 N normal and up to 1.5 N shear. A decoder fitted in a flat configuration transferred to
$R=85$
mm convex and concave mounts with an average RMSE increase of 0.06 N, and a handful of minutes manual calibration against an F/T reference proved sufficient for practical use. Two demonstrations showed the value of the shear channel: a shear-triggered reflex stopped a scalpel before puncturing an inflated balloon in 20 of 20 trials, where normal force alone did not, and adding 3-DoF tactile input to a Diffusion Policy raised plug-insertion success from 48% (vision only) and 64% (normal force only) to 88%.
Several limitations remain. The resistive layer loses sensitivity above roughly 5 N per taxel, bounding the force range, and we did not yet characterize hysteresis, drift, or long-term durability. Future work will therefore examine whether other readily available elastomers or alternative nub geometries can extend this range and sharpen the shear response, as well as quantify time-dependent effects systematically. Furthermore, the general transducer mechanism and fabrication procedure allow for easy form f

actor extension. We have already started designing a VecTile version that can be easily cut into a desired footprint via scissors. Finally, we plan to benchmark VecTile against commercial tactile sensors and to test whether its readings can be mapped into sensor-agnostic tactile representations such as those proposed in
[
25
,
26
]
.

yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force.
We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing.
VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns.

1) 输入三轴接触力

steps.quote:
Each cast silicone nub covers four sensing quadrants and converts a three-axis contact force into four local normal-force signals.
A normal force
$F_{z}$
compresses the nub and raises the four quadrant readings together.
A shear force
$F_{x}$
or
$F_{y}$
tilts the nub and transfers normal load from the trailing side to the leading side.
The mechanism therefore encodes normal force in the balanced response and shear force in the imbalance between opposing quadrant pairs.
